id.2014.1.4.rationale: Integer polynomials must preserve integer right-triangle identities.

br.1992.1.3.reviewed_statement: Given positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, find the polygon $A_0A_1\cdots A_n$ with $A_iA_{i+1} = x_{i+1}$ (indices mod $n$) that has the greatest area.

br.2018.2.4.reviewed_statement: Esmeralda writes $2n$ real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{2n}$, all in the interval $[0, 1]$, around a circle and multiplies all pairs of neighboring numbers, obtaining (counterclockwise) the products $p_1 = x_1x_2,\, p_2 = x_2x_3,\, \ldots,\, p_{2n} = x_{2n}x_1$. She adds the products with even indices and subtracts the products with odd indices. What is the maximum possible value Esmeralda can obtain?
br.2018.2.4.rationale: Cyclic real-variable product optimisation; no metric property of a circle is used.

vn.2000.2.4.reviewed_statement:
For every integer $n \geq 3$ and angle $\alpha$ with $0 < \alpha < \pi$, let $P_n(x) = x^n \sin\alpha - x\sin n\alpha + \sin(n-1)\alpha$.
a) Prove there is a unique polynomial $f(x) = x^2 + ax + b$ dividing $P_n(x)$ for every $n \geq 3$.
b) Prove there is no polynomial $g(x) = x + c$ dividing $P_n(x)$ for every $n \geq 3$.
vn.2000.2.4.rationale: Trigonometric coefficients and common polynomial factors; angles are parameters.

jp.2005.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $P(x, y)$ and $Q(x, y)$ be polynomials in two variables with integer coefficients. For integers $a_0$, $b_0$, define $a_{n+1} = P(a_n, b_n)$, $b_{n+1} = Q(a_n, b_n)$ $(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots)$. Suppose that $(a_1, b_1) \ne (a_0, b_0)$ and that $(a_k, b_k) = (a_0, b_0)$ for some positive integer $k$. Prove that the number of lattice points on the segment with endpoints $(a_n, b_n)$ and $(a_{n+1}, b_{n+1})$ does not depend on $n$.
jp.2005.0.2.rationale: Integer polynomial orbits and lattice-point counts depend on arithmetic coordinates.

jp.2022.0.5.reviewed_statement:
Find the smallest possible value of a positive integer $m$ for which the following statement holds:

$999$ cells are arranged on a circle, and a real number is written in each cell so that, for every cell $A$ and every positive integer $k \le m$, at least one of the following holds:

• the difference between the number in the cell $k$ steps clockwise from $A$ and the number in $A$ is $k$;

• the difference between the number in the cell $k$ steps counterclockwise from $A$ and the number in $A$ is $k$.

Then there exists a cell $S$ such that, if $x$ is the number written in $S$, at least one of the following holds:

• for every positive integer $k < 999$, the number in the cell $k$ steps clockwise from $S$ is $x + k$;

• for every positive integer $k < 999$, the number in the cell $k$ steps counterclockwise from $S$ is $x + k$.
jp.2022.0.5.rationale: Cyclic real arrays and shift constraints; circle denotes indexing.

it.2017.0.1.reviewed_statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Consider a regular hexagon of side $a$, and construct on its sides six rectangles with sides $a$ and $b$, lying outside the hexagon. The twelve new vertices lie on a circle. Repeat the operation with the values of $a$ and $b$ exchanged: start from a regular hexagon of side $b$ and construct on it, again outside the hexagon, six rectangles with sides $a$ and $b$. The twelve new vertices lie on a second circle. Prove that the two circles have the same radius.

tr.2024.1.1.reviewed_statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be a positive integer. A real number is written on each edge of a complete graph with $n$ vertices so that the following conditions hold:

(i) for every triangle of the graph, two of the numbers written on its edges are equal and the third is greater than them;

(ii) defining the weight of a vertex as the sum of the numbers written on the edges leaving that vertex, all vertices have the same weight.

Find all possible values of $n$.
tr.2024.1.1.rationale: Weighted complete graph and vertex sums; triangles denote graph triples.

ru.1994.1.4.reviewed_statement: Real numbers are written in the cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper. Two figures are considered, each consisting of a finite number of cells. The figures may be translated parallel to the grid lines by an integer number of cells. It is known that for every position of the first figure the sum of the numbers in the cells it covers is positive. Prove that there exists a position of the second figure for which the sum of the numbers in the cells it covers is positive.
ru.1994.1.4.rationale: Translated finite grid patterns constrain sums of real entries.

ru.2010.1.4.reviewed_statement:
A positive integer $n \ge 3$ is given. For what smallest $k$ is the following statement true: for any $n$ points $A_i = (x_i, y_i)$ in the plane, no three of which are collinear, and any real numbers $c_i$ $(1 \le i \le n)$, there is a polynomial $P(x, y)$ of degree at most $k$ such that $P(x_i, y_i) = c_i$ for all $i = 1, \dots, n$?

(A polynomial in two variables is a function of the form $P(x, y) = a_{0,0} + a_{1,0}x + a_{0,1}y + a_{2,0}x^2 + a_{1,1}xy + a_{0,2}y^2 + \cdots + a_{k,0}x^k + a_{k-1,1}x^{k-1}y + \cdots + a_{0,k}y^k$. The degree of a nonzero monomial $a_{i,j}x^iy^j$ is $i + j$, and the degree of $P(x, y)$ is the largest degree of its monomials.)
ru.2010.1.4.rationale: Bivariate polynomial interpolation depends on noncollinear point configurations.

ru.2017.2.5.reviewed_statement: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with non-negative coefficients, and let $a$, $b$, $c$ be the side lengths of a triangle. Prove that the numbers $\sqrt[n]{P(a)}$, $\sqrt[n]{P(b)}$, $\sqrt[n]{P(c)}$ are also the side lengths of a triangle.
ru.2017.2.5.rationale: A polynomial transformation preserves triangle inequalities.

ru.2019.1.1.reviewed_statement: A real number $f(A)$ is assigned to every point $A$ of the plane. It is known that if $M$ is the centroid of a triangle $ABC$, then $f(M) = f(A) + f(B) + f(C)$. Prove that $f(A) = 0$ for all points $A$.
ru.2019.1.1.rationale: A functional equation is imposed at triangle centroids.

ru.2021.1.2.reviewed_statement: Let $P(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ with non-negative coefficients such that the function $y = P(x)$ is odd. Can it happen that for distinct points $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ of the graph $G: y = P(x)$ the tangent to $G$ at $A_1$ passes through $A_2$, the tangent at $A_2$ passes through $A_3$, $\dots$, and the tangent at $A_n$ passes through $A_1$?
ru.2021.1.2.rationale: Polynomial derivatives and tangents to a function graph.

es.2002.1.2.reviewed_statement:
In a triangle $ABC$, $A'$ is the foot of the altitude from vertex $A$ and $H$ is the orthocenter.

a) Given a positive real number $k$ such that $\dfrac{AA'}{HA'}=k$, find the relation between the angles $B$ and $C$ as a function of $k$.

b) If $B$ and $C$ are fixed, find the locus of the vertex $A$ for each value of $k$.
es.2002.1.2.rationale: Altitude, orthocentre and an angle locus; k is a geometric ratio.

es.2004.1.1.reviewed_statement: We have a set of $221$ real numbers whose sum is $110721$. They are arranged forming a rectangle in such a way that all the rows and the first and last columns are arithmetic progressions of more than one element. Prove that the sum of the elements in the four corners equals $2004$.
es.2004.1.1.rationale: Arithmetic progressions in a rectangular array; rectangle is an indexing layout.

es.2010.1.3.reviewed_statement: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. The angle $\angle APD = 60^\circ$. Let $E$, $F$, $G$ and $H$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$, respectively. Find the greatest positive real number $k$ such that $$EG + 3HF \ge kd + (1-k)s,$$ where $s$ is the semiperimeter of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ and $d$ is the sum of the lengths of its diagonals. When does equality hold?
es.2010.1.3.rationale: Optimising a geometric length inequality over a coefficient.

es.2013.1.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $k$ and $n$ be integers with $n \ge k \ge 3$. Consider $n+1$ points in the plane, no three of which are collinear. Each segment joining two of these points is assigned a color from among $k$ given colors.

An angle is called *bicolored* if its vertex is one of the $n+1$ points and its sides are two of the above segments having different colors.

Prove that there exists a coloring such that the number of *bicolored* angles is strictly greater than $$n\left\lfloor \frac{n}{k} \right\rfloor^2 \binom{k}{2}.$$

REMARK: $\lfloor t \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of the real number $t$, that is, the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$.
es.2013.1.3.rationale: Counting coloured edges and bichromatic triples; the metric embedding is incidental.

es.2015.1.1.reviewed_statement: On the graph of a polynomial function with integer coefficients, two points with integer coordinates are chosen. Prove that if the distance between them is an integer, then the segment joining them is parallel to the $x$-axis.
es.2015.1.1.rationale: Integer polynomial values and integer Euclidean distance impose arithmetic constraints.

cz.2017.1.2.reviewed_statement: Find all pairs of real numbers $k$, $l$ such that the inequality $$ka^2+lb^2>c^2$$ holds for the side lengths $a$, $b$, $c$ of any triangle.
cz.2017.1.2.rationale: Characterisation of coefficients in an inequality for all triangle sides.

cz.2018.1.2.reviewed_statement: Real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ are chosen so that the numbers $$\frac{1}{|x^2+2yz|},\quad \frac{1}{|y^2+2zx|},\quad \frac{1}{|z^2+2xy|}$$ are the side lengths of a (non-degenerate) triangle. Determine all possible values of the expression $xy+yz+zx$.
cz.2018.1.2.rationale: Algebraic expressions constrained to be triangle sides.

ut.2021.1.2.reviewed_statement:
Points $A$, $V_1$, $V_2$, $B$, $U_2$, $U_1$ lie fixed on a circle $\Gamma$, in that order, and such that $BU_2 > AU_1 > BV_2 > AV_1$.
Let $X$ be a variable point on the arc $V_1V_2$ of $\Gamma$ not containing $A$ or $B$. Line $XA$ meets line $U_1V_1$ at $C$, while line $XB$ meets line $U_2V_2$ at $D$. Let $O$ and $\rho$ denote the circumcenter and circumradius of $\triangle XCD$, respectively.
Prove there exists a fixed point $K$ and a real number $c$, independent of $X$, for which $OK^2 - \rho^2 = c$ always holds regardless of the choice of $X$.
ut.2021.1.2.rationale: Circumcircle centres, radii and a fixed geometric point.

ut.2023.2.5.reviewed_statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be fixed positive integers. Tsvety and Freyja play a game on an infinite grid of unit square cells. Tsvety has secretly written a real number inside of each cell so that the sum of the numbers within every rectangle of size either $m \times n$ or $n \times m$ is zero. Freyja wants to learn all of these numbers.
One by one, Freyja asks Tsvety about some cell in the grid, and Tsvety truthfully reveals what number is written in it. Freyja wins if, at any point, Freyja can simultaneously deduce the number written in every cell of the entire infinite grid. (If this never occurs, Freyja has lost the game and Tsvety wins.)
In terms of $m$ and $n$, find the smallest number of questions that Freyja must ask to win, or show that no finite number of questions can suffice.
ut.2023.2.5.rationale: Rectangle sums in an infinite real array and minimum information queries.

hr.2023.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Do there exist pairwise distinct positive real numbers $a_1,a_3,a_5,\dots,a_{2023}$ such that from

one square of side length $a_1$,

three squares of side length $a_3$, $\dots$,

$k$ squares of side length $a_k$, $\dots$,

$2023$ squares of side length $a_{2023}$

a square can be assembled?
hr.2023.0.3.rationale: Assembling prescribed square pieces into a square.

no.2015.0.2.reviewed_statement:
a. King Arthur is placing $a + b + c$ knights around a table. $a$ knights are dressed in red, $b$ knights are dressed in brown, and $c$ knights are dressed in orange.

Arthur wishes to arrange the knights so that no knight is seated next to someone dressed in the same colour as himself. Show that this is possible if, and only if, there exists a triangle whose sides have lengths $a + \frac{1}{2}$, $b + \frac{1}{2}$, and $c + \frac{1}{2}$.

b. Nils is playing a game with a bag originally containing $n$ red and one black marble. He begins with a fortune equal to $1$.

In each move he picks a real number $x$ with $0 \le x \le y$, where his present fortune is $y$. Then he draws a marble from the bag. If the marble is red, his fortune increases by $x$, but if it is black, it decreases by $x$. The game is over after $n$ moves when there is only a single marble left.

In each move Nils chooses $x$ so that he ensures a final fortune greater or equal to $Y$. What is the largest possible value of $Y$?
no.2015.0.2.rationale: The alternatives concern cyclic colouring and a betting optimisation; triangle inequality is an equivalent numerical condition.

no.2019.0.3.reviewed_statement:
a. Three circles are pairwise tangent, with none of them lying inside another. The centres of the circles are the corners of a triangle with circumference $1$. What is the smallest possible value for the sum of the areas of the circles?

b. Find all real functions $f$ defined on the real numbers except zero, satisfying $f(2019) = 1$ and $$f(x)f(y) + f\left(\frac{2019}{x}\right)f\left(\frac{2019}{y}\right) = 2f(xy)$$ for all $x, y \ne 0$.
no.2019.0.3.rationale: Separate alternatives: circle-area optimisation and a functional equation.

no.2023.0.4.reviewed_statement:
a. Assuming $a$, $b$, and $c$ are the side lengths of a triangle, show that $$\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{ab} + \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{bc} + \frac{c^2+a^2-b^2}{ca} > 2.$$ Also show that the inequality does not necessarily hold if you replace $2$ (on the right hand side) by a bigger number.

b. Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ satisfying $$f\big(f(x) + y\big) = f(y) + x \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \mathbb{R}_+.$$ (Here $\mathbb{R}_+$ is the set of all real numbers $x > 0$.)
no.2023.0.4.rationale: Separate alternatives: triangle inequality and a functional equation.

ukt.1993.1.3.reviewed_statement:
Six rods $A_1A_2$, $A_2A_3$, $A_3A_4$, $A_4A_5$, $A_5A_6$, $A_6A_1$ of lengths $(a_1+a_2)$, $(a_2+a_3)$, $(a_3+a_4)$, $(a_4+a_5)$, $(a_5+a_6)$, $(a_6+a_1)$ respectively, where $a_i > 0$ $(i = 1, 2, \dots, 6)$, are freely jointed together to form a hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$. Prove that the hexagon can be adjusted so that it takes the shape of a convex hexagon circumscribing a circle.
Prove also that if the real numbers $a_i$ $(i = 1, 2, \dots, 6)$ are permuted amongst themselves in any way, the six new resulting rods have the same property and that whatever permutation is made the inscribed circle always has the same radius. Find the radius explicitly in terms of elementary symmetric functions of $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_6$.
Does there exist a convex hexagon, with side lengths $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ in some order, circumscribing a circle?
ukt.1993.1.3.rationale: Tangential hexagon geometry linked to symmetric algebraic expressions.

ukt.2015.3.9.reviewed_statement: Consider a circle $\Gamma$ with three fixed points $A$, $B$ and $C$ on $\Gamma$. Also fix a real number $\lambda \in (0, 1)$. Let $P$ denote a variable point on $\Gamma$ with $P \notin \{A, B, C\}$, and let $M$ be the point on the segment $CP$ such that $CM = \lambda \cdot CP$. Let $Q$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $AMP$ and $BMC$. Prove that, as $P$ varies, the point $Q$ lies on a fixed circle.
ukt.2015.3.9.rationale: A moving-point circle locus; lambda is a geometric parameter.

nlt.2021.2.8.reviewed_statement: Determine all positive integers $n$ with the following property: for every triple $(a,b,c)$ of positive real numbers there is a triple $(k,\ell,m)$ of non-negative integers such that $an^k$, $bn^\ell$ and $cn^m$ are the lengths of the sides of a (non-degenerate) triangle.

nlt.2026.2.5.reviewed_statement:
Five real numbers are placed around a circle. Each number is $1$ less than the product of its two neighbours. The sum of the five numbers is $0$. What are the possible values of the product of the five numbers?

The beloved Governor Henning is in charge of building bridges between every pair of islands that are a distance of $1$ apart. For every island $i$, Henning chooses two real numbers $x_i$ and $y_i$ that satisfy $x_i^2 + y_i^2 = 1$. The cost of a bridge between islands $i$ and $j$ is then given by $1 + x_ix_j + y_iy_j$. cht.2025.2.5.reviewed_statement:

de.2025.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Determine all real numbers $t$ with $0 < t < 1$ for which the following statement is true: if in an acute-angled triangle the sides of lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$ are, as usual, opposite the angles of sizes $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$, respectively, and $\frac{a}{b+c} = t$ holds, then $\alpha \le \beta$ and $\alpha \le \gamma$.

Remark: The correctness of the answer must be proved.

de.2026.0.3.reviewed_statement:
An equilateral triangle $ABC$ with area $1$ and a real number $q$ with $0 < q < 1$ are given. A point $P$ of the triangle $ABC$ is colored green if every triangle with area $q$ which is part of the triangle $ABC$ contains the point $P$. Determine the area of the green part of the triangle $ABC$ in terms of $q$.

Note: Every triangle includes the points of its boundary and all interior points.
de.2026.0.3.rationale: Intersection areas of subtriangles in an equilateral triangle.

dem.1971.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Definition: A set $M$ of elements $u, v, w, \dots$ is called a group with respect to the algebraic operation $A$ if and only if the following three conditions are satisfied:
(a) To every ordered pair $[u, v]$ of elements of $M$, an element $w$ of $M$ is assigned by the operation $A$ (one writes $u \circ v = w$).
(b) The algebraic operation $A$ is associative, i.e. for all elements $u, v, w$ of $M$: $(u \circ v) \circ w = u \circ (v \circ w)$.
(c) For any two elements $u$ and $v$ of $M$ there exists at least one element $x$ of $M$ such that $u \circ x = v$, and at least one element $y$ of $M$ such that $y \circ u = v$.
Now let $P$ be the set of all polynomials of first degree $f(x) = a_0 + a_1x$, where $a_0, a_1$ are rational numbers and $a_1 \neq 0$. Furthermore, let an algebraic operation $A$ be defined in $P$ as follows: if $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are polynomials of $P$, then $f(x) \circ g(x) = g[f(x)]$. Decide whether $P$ is a group with respect to $A$.

Version B. On level terrain, an arc of a circle of radius $r$ is staked out, when in addition a tangent $t$ to this arc and its point of tangency $A$ are known, as follows: at arbitrary points $P'$ of $t$ (with $\overline{AP'} = x < r$) perpendiculars to $t$ are erected, and on them (on the side of $t$ on which the arc lies) segments $P'P$ are marked off such that the points $P$ are points of the desired arc. Here $\overline{P'P} = y < r$.
(a) Prove that then $y = \frac{x^2}{2r-y}$.
(b) In practice it often suffices to determine approximate values of $y$. This is done as follows: a first approximation $y_1$ is obtained from the equation $y_1 = \frac{x^2}{2r}$. If its accuracy is not sufficient, a second approximation $y_2$ is determined from the equation $y_2 = \frac{x^2}{2r - y_1}$. One can proceed analogously until the required accuracy is reached.
Investigate whether there is a smallest natural number $n$ with the property that for all positive real numbers $x \le \frac{1}{n}r$ the relative error $\delta = \frac{|y - y_1|}{r}$ of the approximation $y_1 = \frac{x^2}{2r}$ is not greater than $0.001$, i.e. that $\delta \le 0.001$.
dem.1971.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: affine composition and circle-arc approximation.

dem.1973.0.5.reviewed_statement: Someone wrote a real number on each of the six faces of a cube, where the numbers $0$ and $1$ were among these $6$ numbers. Then he replaced each of these $6$ numbers by the arithmetic mean of the four numbers which had previously been on the $4$ adjacent faces. (He remembered each old number to be replaced, even after it had been replaced, as long as it was still needed for forming the means for the numbers of its adjacent faces.) With the $6$ new numbers obtained in this way, he repeated this operation. In total he carried it out twenty-five times. At the end he found that on each face he again had the same number as at the beginning. Could he have obtained this result with correct calculation?
dem.1973.0.5.rationale: Averaging real labels on the cube adjacency graph.

dem.1977.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Give all polynomials $f(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \dots + a_nx^n$ with real coefficients $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n$ which have the following property: for all real numbers $x$, $x\cdot f(x-1) = (x-2)\cdot f(x)$.

Version B. For every natural number $n \ge 5$, give a dissection of a regular convex $n$-gon into a minimal number of
(a) triangles which are all acute-angled,
(b) triangles which are all obtuse-angled.
Note: A dissection into triangles means a dissection of the $n$-gon in which each side of a dissection triangle is either at the same time a side of another dissection triangle or one of the sides of the $n$-gon.
dem.1977.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: polynomial equation and polygon dissections.

dem.1978.0.4.reviewed_statement:
Definition: Let $d(X, Y)$ denote the distance of two points $X, Y$ of a point set $\mathfrak{M}$. A real number $d$ is called the diameter of $\mathfrak{M}$ if the following conditions are satisfied:
(1) For any two points $X, Y$ of $\mathfrak{M}$, $d(X, Y) \le d$.
(2) There are points $P, Q$ of $\mathfrak{M}$ for which $d(P, Q) = d$.
Prove:
(a) If a disk with diameter $d$ is divided into two parts by an arbitrary polygonal line which intersects the circle at a point $M$ and a point $N$, then one of these partial regions (each understood including its boundary) also has diameter $d$.
(b) If a solid ball with diameter $d$ is divided by a plane cut $\varepsilon_1$ into two parts and then one of these parts is again divided into two parts by a plane cut $\varepsilon_2$, then for every such dissection of a ball into three parts at least one of these parts (each understood including its bounding surfaces) also has diameter $d$.
dem.1978.0.4.rationale: Diameters of pieces from disk/sphere cuts; real lengths are geometric data.

dem.1978.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Let $n$ be a positive number, and let $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be an $n$-tuple of real numbers with $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n$. Investigate whether for these given $a_1, \dots, a_n$ there is a real number $x$ such that the number
$$z = |x - a_1| + |x - a_2| + \dots + |x - a_n|$$
is as small as possible. If there is such an $x$, determine all real numbers $x$ with this property and state the corresponding minimal value of $z$.

Version B. (a) Let a natural number $n \ge 2$ be given. Let $u$ be the circumcircle of a regular $2n$-gon $A_0A_1\dots A_{2n-1}$. A set of three vertices $A_i, A_j, A_k$ of this $2n$-gon is called one-sided if there is a semicircular arc $h$ on the circle $u$, including its two endpoints, which contains $A_i$, $A_j$ and $A_k$. Determine the probability $w_n$ that an arbitrarily chosen set $M = \{A_i, A_j, A_k\}$ of three vertices is one-sided.
(b) Determine the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty} w_n$, if it exists.
Note: If $m_n$ is the number of all sets that can be formed from three vertices $A_i, A_j, A_k$ of the $2n$-gon, and $g_n$ is the number of all one-sided ones among them, then the probability sought in (a) is defined as $w_n = \frac{g_n}{m_n}$.
dem.1978.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: absolute-distance minimisation and polygon probability.

dem.1979.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Let $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ be a regular pentagon with given side length $s$. Around each point $A_i$ ($i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$) let the sphere $K_i$ with radius $\frac{s}{2}$ and center $A_i$ be placed. Then in the set of those spheres $K'$ which have the property of touching each of the five spheres $K_i$, there are exactly two spheres $K_1'$ and $K_2'$ with radius $\frac{s}{2}$. Investigate whether $K_1'$ and $K_2'$ intersect, touch, or have no point in common.

Version B. (a) Let $M$ be the set of all triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers for which the following inequalities (1) to (5) are satisfied:
$$\begin{aligned} 55x + z &\le 54 &(1)\\ 55y + z &\le 54 &(2)\\ 55x - 4z &\ge 4 &(3)\\ 55y - 4z &\ge 4 &(4)\\ z &\ge -1 &(5) \end{aligned}$$
Investigate whether for the expression
$$f(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \qquad (6)$$
there exists a triple $(x_0, y_0, z_0) \in M$ with the property that for all triples $(x, y, z) \in M$ the inequality $f(x_0, y_0, z_0) \ge f(x, y, z)$ holds. If this is the case, determine $f(x_0, y_0, z_0)$.
(b) Let $M'$ be the set of all triples $(x, y, z)$ of integers for which the inequalities (1) to (5) are satisfied. Investigate whether for the expression (6) there exists a triple $(x_1, y_1, z_1) \in M'$ with the property that for all triples $(x, y, z) \in M'$ the inequality $f(x_1, y_1, z_1) \ge f(x, y, z)$ holds. If this is the case, determine $f(x_1, y_1, z_1)$.
dem.1979.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: sphere tangency and quadratic optimisation.

dem.1982.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. (a) Prove: if
$$a = \overline{BC}, \quad b = \overline{AC}, \quad c = \overline{AB}, \quad d = \overline{AD}, \quad e = \overline{BD}, \quad f = \overline{CD} \qquad (1)$$
are the edge lengths of a tetrahedron $ABCD$, then the surface area $A_O$ of this tetrahedron satisfies the inequality
$$A_O < \frac13\left(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 + e^2 + f^2\right). \qquad (2)$$
(b) Investigate whether the statement about (2) can be sharpened to the following statement: there is a smallest real number $\lambda$ with $\lambda < \frac13$ such that for the surface area $A_O$ of every tetrahedron $ABCD$, denoting its edge lengths as in (1), the inequality
$$A_O \le \lambda\left(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 + e^2 + f^2\right) \qquad (3)$$
holds. If this is the case, determine this number $\lambda$.

Version B. Determine all those functions $f$ and $g$ which are defined for all non-negative real numbers $x$, have real function values and satisfy the following conditions:
(1) For all $x \ge 0$: $f(x) \ge 1$ and $g(x) \ge 0$.
(2) For all $x \ge 0$: $(f(x))^2 - (g(x))^2 = 1$.
(3) For all $x \ge 0$ and all $y \ge 0$: $f\left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) = f(x)\cdot f(y) + g(x)\cdot g(y)$.
(4) For all $x \ge 0$ and all $y \ge 0$: $g\left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) = f(x)\cdot g(y) + g(x)\cdot f(y)$.
dem.1982.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: tetrahedron inequality and functional equation.

dem.1983.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Let $ABCD$ be a tetrahedron in which the three edges $AD$, $BD$ and $CD$ are pairwise perpendicular. Let the lengths of these edges $AD$, $BD$ and $CD$ be denoted by $a$, $b$ and $c$, respectively. Furthermore, let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the boundary of the triangle $ABC$, and let $g$ be the line through $D$ and $P$.
(a) Prove that then for the sum $s$ of the distances of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ from $g$ always
$$s \le \sqrt{2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)} \qquad (1)$$
holds.
(b) Investigate (in terms of the given edge lengths $a, b, c$) whether there is a point $P$ such that equality holds in (1). If this is the case, determine (in terms of $a, b, c$) all these points $P$.

Version B. In the investigation of frequency distributions in mathematical statistics, functions occur which are defined for finitely many natural numbers and which are required to satisfy so-called functional equations (equations between different function values). An example is the following: let a natural number $n \ge 2$ and a real number $p$ with $0 < p < 1$ be given. Determine (in terms of $n$ and $p$) those functions $f$ with the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ as domain which, for $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$, satisfy the following equation (1):
$$\sum_{x=0}^{n} x\cdot(x-1)\cdot(x-2)\cdot\ldots\cdot(x-k+1)\cdot f(x) = n\cdot(n-1)\cdot(n-2)\cdot\ldots\cdot(n-k+1)\cdot p^k. \qquad (1)$$
Note: For $k = 1$, equation (1) is to be understood as $\sum_{x=0}^{n} x\cdot f(x) = n\cdot p$.
dem.1983.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: tetrahedron distance bounds and finite functional moment identities.

dem.1987.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. In a mathematics camp, a group leader proposes to the $n$ students ($n \ge 3$) of his group to choose the student who is to do the blackboard duty by the following method: the students are numbered $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and stand in a circle in this order, where (in the direction $P_1, P_2, \dots$) $P_n$ is again followed by $P_1$. First a coin toss decides whether $P_1$ or $P_2$ leaves the circle: if heads is up, $P_1$ leaves, if tails, $P_2$. Then the elimination is continued with those two students not yet eliminated who follow, in the stated direction, the student just eliminated last. On heads, again the first of these two in that direction leaves, on tails the second. This is repeated until only one student remains, who is then designated to be on duty.
(a) In the case $n = 3$, compute the probabilities $W_1$, $W_2$, $W_3$ that $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$, respectively, are designated to be on duty.
(b) Prove for every $n \ge 3$ that the selection method is unfair, i.e. that the probability of being designated to be on duty is not the same for all students $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$.
Remark: If some random event $A$ occurs as a consequence of any one of $m$ events out of a total of $N$ possible events (which are mutually exclusive and equally likely), then the number $p = \frac{m}{N}$ is called the probability of the event $A$.

Version B. Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{1987}$ be non-negative real numbers for which the sum of the squares equals $10$ and the sum of the cubes is greater than $1$. Investigate whether under these assumptions it is always possible to select
(a) $9$ of these numbers,
(b) $10$ of these numbers
such that the sum of the selected numbers is greater than $1$. (If a number occurs several times among $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{1987}$, it may be included among the selected numbers at most as often.)
dem.1987.0.6.rationale: Probability and real-variable subset inequalities; cubes are third powers.

dem.1989.0.6.reviewed_statement:
(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Prove: for every natural number $n > 1$ and for any $n + 2$ real numbers $p, q, a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ which satisfy
$$0 < p \le a_i \le q \quad (i = 1, 2, \dots, n), \qquad (1)$$
the two inequalities
$$n^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_k}\right) \le n^2 + \left[\frac{n^2}{4}\right]\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{p}{q}} - \sqrt{\frac{q}{p}}\right)^2 \qquad (2)$$
hold.
Note: For real $x$, as usual, $[x]$ denotes the integer $[x] = g$ with $g \le x < g + 1$.
Furthermore, for given $n, p, q$ with $0 < p \le q$, determine all those $a_i$ satisfying (1) for which in (2) equality holds
(a) between the first and the second number,
(b) between the second and the third number.

Version B. Determine the largest possible number of squares of side length $1$ which can be placed in a given square of side length $1.99$ without protruding beyond its boundary and without overlapping each other.
dem.1989.0.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: real inequalities and square packing.

dem.1996.2.6.reviewed_statement:
Part A. Prove the following statement: if a polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + Ax^2 + Bx + C$ has three real positive roots, at least two of which are different from each other, then $A^2 + B^2 + 18C > 0$.

Part B. Every point of a plane is coloured with exactly one of the three colours red, black or blue. Prove that under this assumption there always exists a rectangle in this plane whose four vertices all have the same colour.
dem.1996.2.6.rationale: Separate alternatives: polynomial root inequality and plane colouring.

dem.2018.1.2.reviewed_statement: About a tetrahedron it is known that two edges have length $a$ and the other four edges have length $b$, where $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary positive real numbers. Which values can the ratio $v = a/b$ of the edge lengths take?
dem.2018.1.2.rationale: Existence of a tetrahedron with prescribed edge lengths.

dem.2018.2.4.reviewed_statement:
(a) Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the side lengths of a triangle with perimeter $4$. Prove that then
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + abc < 8.$$

(b) Is there a real number $d < 8$ such that for every triangle with perimeter $4$ the inequality
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + abc < d \qquad (1)$$
holds, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ denote the side lengths of the triangle?
dem.2018.2.4.rationale: Optimising a polynomial expression in triangle sides.

ro.2019.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Determine the natural numbers $n \ge 4$ for which the following property holds: any distinct nonzero complex numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying
$$(a - b)^n + (b - c)^n + (c - a)^n = 0$$
are the affixes of the vertices of an equilateral triangle.
ro.2019.0.3.rationale: Complex power sums constrain an equilateral triangle.

ltt.2014.1.3.reviewed_statement:
Positive real numbers $a,b$ and $c$ are given such that the system of equations
$$\begin{cases} a^2x+b^2y+c^2z=1,\\ xy+yz+zx=1 \end{cases}$$
has a unique real solution $(x,y,z)$. Prove that there exists a triangle with side lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$.
ltt.2014.1.3.rationale: Uniqueness of a real algebraic system constrains triangle-side coefficients.

eet.2016.1.6.reviewed_statement: A circle is divided into arcs of equal size by $n$ points ($n\ge 1$). For any positive integer $x$, let $P_n(x)$ denote the number of possibilities for colouring all those points, using colours from $x$ given colours, so that any rotation of the colouring by $i\cdot\frac{360^\circ}{n}$, where $i$ is a positive integer less than $n$, gives a colouring that differs from the original in at least one point. Prove that the function $P_n(x)$ is a polynomial with respect to $x$.
eet.2016.1.6.rationale: Counting primitive cyclic colourings by a polynomial; circular order is discrete.

fi.2025.0.1.reviewed_statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ denote the altitudes of a triangle $A$.
(1) Let $r>0$ be a real number. Show that there exists a triangle $A$ with area $\frac12$ for which $abc<r$.
(2) Show that for all triangles $A$ with area $\frac12$ it holds that $abc<1$.
fi.2025.0.1.rationale: Triangle altitudes and fixed area; a real bound alone does not establish algebra.

frt.2014.3.9.reviewed_statement: Determine all real numbers $t$ such that, whenever $a,b,c$ are the side lengths of a non-degenerate triangle, the same holds for $a^2+bct$, $b^2+cat$, $c^2+abt$.
frt.2014.3.9.rationale: Algebraic parameter transformation must preserve all triangles.

frt.2019.4.10.rationale: Packing disjoint inscribed triangles with a perimeter threshold.

ee.1998.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $BC$ be the longest side of a triangle $ABC$, and let the angle bisector drawn from the vertex $A$ meet the side $BC$ at the point $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from the point $D$ to the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Denote by $R$ the ratio of the areas of the triangles $DEB$ and $DFC$.

a) Prove that for every positive real number $r$ one can construct a triangle $ABC$ for which the ratio $R$ equals the given number $r$.

b) Prove that if the ratio $R$ is irrational, then at least one of the side lengths of the triangle $ABC$ is irrational.

c) Give examples of triangles in which the lengths of exactly one, exactly two, or all three sides are irrational, but the ratio $R$ is rational.
ee.1998.0.3.rationale: Triangle projections and area ratios are tied to rational/irrational side relations.

ee.2002.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Prove that positive real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the inequality
$$2(a^4 + b^4 + c^4) < (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)^2$$
if and only if there exists a triangle with side lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$.
ee.2002.0.3.rationale: A symmetric quartic inequality characterises triangle inequalities.

ee.2007.0.2.reviewed_statement: Positive real numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are such that for every positive integer $n$ the numbers $x^n$, $y^n$ and $z^n$ are the side lengths of some triangle. Prove that at least two of the numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are equal.
ee.2007.0.2.rationale: All power transforms must remain triangle sides.

ee.2010.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the side lengths of a triangle and $k$ a real number. Prove that if the quadratic equation $x^2 + (a + b + c)x + k(ab + bc + ca) = 0$ has a real solution, then $k < 1$.
ee.2010.0.2.rationale: A discriminant constraint is combined with triangle inequalities.

ee.2012.0.5.reviewed_statement:
a) Does there exist a function defined on the set of all real numbers with real values, not identically zero, such that reflecting its graph in the $y$-axis gives the graph of the derivative of this function?

b) Does there exist a function defined on the set of all real numbers with real values, not identically zero, such that shifting its graph by $1$ unit along the $x$-axis in the positive direction gives the graph of the derivative of this function?
ee.2012.0.5.rationale: Function graph transformations and derivatives; no Euclidean geometric theorem.

huo.2009.0.2.reviewed_statement: Project the regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ orthogonally onto a number line lying in space, and let the projections of the vertices be the real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, respectively. Express the edge length of the tetrahedron in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$.
huo.2009.0.2.rationale: Tetrahedron projections relate coordinate expressions to edge lengths.

um.2001.0.6.reviewed_statement: Each point in the plane is assigned a real number such that, for any triangle, the number at the center of its inscribed circle is equal to the arithmetic mean of the three numbers at its vertices. Prove that all points in the plane are assigned the same number.
um.2001.0.6.rationale: A functional equation is imposed at circle centres.

um.2012.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find all integers $n \ge 3$ such that among any $n$ positive real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $$\max(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) \le n\cdot\min(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n),$$ there exist three that are the side lengths of an acute triangle.
um.2012.0.1.rationale: Selecting an acute triangle from reals subject to ratio bounds.

um.2025.0.6.reviewed_statement: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $m \ge n$. There are $m$ cupcakes of different flavors arranged around a circle and $n$ people who like cupcakes. Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least 1. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least 1 with respect to $P$.
um.2025.0.6.rationale: Fair division of cyclic real valuations; circle denotes order.

ar.2005.0.4.reviewed_statement: We will say that a positive integer is a winner if it can be written as the sum of a perfect square plus a perfect cube. For example, 33is a winner because 33 = 52+ 23. Gabriel chooses two positive integers, r and s, and Germ án must find 2005 positive integers n such that for each n, the numbers r+nands+nare winners. Prove that Germ án can always achieve his goal.
ar.2005.0.4.rationale: Squares and cubes are integer powers in an additive construction.

sg.2010.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $(a_n)$, $(b_n)$, $n = 1, 2, \ldots$ be two sequences of integers defined by $a_1 = 1$, $b_1 = 0$ and for $n \geq 1$ $$a_{n+1} = 7a_n + 12b_n + 6 \quad b_{n+1} = 4a_n + 7b_n + 3$$ Prove that $a_n^2$ is the difference of two consecutive cubes.
sg.2010.0.2.rationale: Integer recurrences and consecutive third powers.

sg.2018.0.1.reviewed_statement: Consider a regular cube with side length 2. Let $A$ and $B$ be 2 vertices that are furthest apart. Construct a sequence of points on the surface of the cube $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k$ so that $A_1 = A$, $A_k = B$ and for any $i = 1, \ldots, k - 1$, the distance from $A_i$ to $A_{i+1}$ is 3. Find the minimum value of $k$.
sg.2018.0.1.rationale: Minimum jumps constrained by the cube surface.

uk1.2011.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $s$ be an integer greater than 6. A solid cube of side $s$ has a square hole of side $x<6$ drilled straight through between opposite faces. The volume of the remaining solid equals, numerically, its total surface area. Find all possible integer values of $x$.
uk1.2011.0.2.rationale: An integer-length drilled solid gives a volume/surface Diophantine condition.

ie.2005.0.1.reviewed_statement: Prove that $2005^{2005}$ is a sum of two perfect squares, but not the sum of two perfect cubes.
ie.2005.0.1.rationale: Representations as sums of square and cube powers.

id.2011.2.5.reviewed_statement: A unit cube is labeled with numbers as shown. Place $2^n$ such cubes to form a $1 \times 2 \times n$ cuboid on a floor. Let $S$ be the sum of all visible numbers (not facing the floor). Find the minimum $n$ such that there exists a placement with $S > 2011$.
id.2011.2.5.rationale: Counting visible labels in cube arrangements; the stored cube-count notation needs separate source checking.

br.1981.0.6.reviewed_statement: The centers of the faces of a cube form a regular octahedron of volume $V$. Through each vertex of the cube take the plane perpendicular to the long diagonal from that vertex. These planes also form a regular octahedron. Show that its volume is $27V$.
br.1981.0.6.rationale: Volumes of a cube and octahedral construction.

br.1994.1.1.reviewed_statement:
The edges of a cube are labeled from $1$ to $12$ in an arbitrary manner.

a) Show that it is not possible to make the sum of edge-labels at each vertex the same.

b) Show that if one of the labels is changed to $13$, we can label the edges so that all eight vertices have the same sum.
br.1994.1.1.rationale: Distinct edge labels and vertex sums on a cube graph.

br.2002.1.1.reviewed_statement: Show that there is a set of $2002$ distinct positive integers such that the sum of one or more elements of the set is never a perfect square, cube, or higher power.
br.2002.1.1.rationale: Constructing distinct integers with subset sums avoiding perfect powers.

br.2005.1.3.reviewed_statement: A square is contained in a cube when all of its points lie on the faces or in the interior of the cube. Determine the largest $\ell > 0$ such that there exists a square of side $\ell$ contained in a cube with edge length $1$.
br.2005.1.3.rationale: Largest square contained in a cube.

br.2010.1.3.reviewed_statement: What is the largest shadow that a cube of side length $1$ can cast, with the sun directly overhead? (The shadow is the largest possible area of the orthogonal projection of the cube onto a plane.)
br.2010.1.3.rationale: Maximum area of an orthogonal cube projection.

vn.1970.0.5.reviewed_statement: A plane $p$ passes through a vertex of a cube so that the three edges at that vertex make equal angles with $p$. Find the cosine of this angle. Find the positions of the feet of perpendiculars from the vertices onto $p$. Among the 28 lines through two vertices and the 20 planes through three vertices of the cube, find some relationship with $p$.
vn.1970.0.5.rationale: Plane angles, perpendicular feet and cube incidence.

vn.1971.0.2.reviewed_statement: $ABCDA'B'C'D'$ is a cube. $L$ is a line intersecting or parallel to lines $AA'$, $BC$, and $DB'$. $L$ meets $BC$ at $M$ with $|BM|=m$. Show $|B'E|=m$ and $|D'F|=m$ where $E,F$ are defined by certain planes. Construct $P = L \cap A'B'C'D'$. Find distances from $P$ to lines $A'B'$ and $A'D'$ and a relation independent of $m$. Find the locus of $M$ and the envelope $S$ of $L$.
vn.1971.0.2.rationale: Spatial loci/envelopes in a cube; the abbreviated plane definitions need separate source checking.

vn.1974.0.4.reviewed_statement: A unit cube $C$ has 12 edges. The lines containing the 12 edges meet a plane $p$ in 12 points. What can you say about the 12 points?

vn.1982.2.6.reviewed_statement: Let $ABCDA'B'C'D'$ be a cube (with faces $ABCD$ and $A'B'C'D'$, and edges $AA', BB', CC', DD'$). Consider the four lines $AA'$, $BC$, $D'C'$, and the line joining the midpoints of $BB'$ and $DD'$. Show that no line cuts all four of these lines.
vn.1982.2.6.rationale: Spatial lines and existence of a transversal.

vn.1997.2.6.reviewed_statement: In the unit cube, 75 points are given with no three collinear. Prove that there exists a triangle with vertices among these 75 points whose area does not exceed $\dfrac{7}{72}$.
vn.1997.2.6.rationale: Point selection with triangle-area bounds inside a cube.

ru.2019.2.8.reviewed_statement: A positive integer $n$ is given. A $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cube is assembled from $26$ white unit cubes and one black unit cube, with the black cube at its center. From $n^3$ such cubes with edge $3$, a cube with edge $3n$ is assembled. What is the smallest number of white unit cubes that can be repainted red so that every white unit cube has at least one common vertex with some red one?
ru.2019.2.8.rationale: Minimum domination of a finite cube adjacency grid.

ru.2025.1.4.reviewed_statement: A positive integer $N$ is given. A cube with side $2N + 1$ is made of $(2N+1)^3$ unit cubes, each of which is black or white. It turned out that among any $8$ unit cubes having a common vertex and forming a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ cube there are at most $4$ black cubes. What is the largest possible number of black cubes?
ru.2025.1.4.rationale: Extremal black/white counts in overlapping discrete blocks.

pl.2012.1.2.reviewed_statement: Determine all pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers for which a cube $K$ with edge $n$ can be surrounded by rectangular blocks of dimensions $m \times 1 \times 1$ in such a way that a cube with edge $n+2$ is formed, having the same center as $K$.
pl.2012.1.2.rationale: Tiling a spatial cube shell with rods.

es.2006.2.5.reviewed_statement: Prove that the product of four consecutive natural numbers can be neither a perfect square nor a perfect cube.
es.2006.2.5.rationale: Products of consecutive integers cannot be square/cube powers.

es.2023.1.1.reviewed_statement:
We have a cube of side $3$ made up of $27$ cubic pieces of side $1$. Inside each piece there is a light bulb that can be on or off. Each time a piece is pressed (it is not possible to press the one at the center of the cube), the state of its bulb changes, as well as the states of the bulbs of the pieces that share a face with the pressed one. Initially, all the bulbs are off. Answer the following questions, with justification:

(1) Is it possible to get all the bulbs to be on?

(2) Is it possible to get all the bulbs to be on except the one at the center of the cube?

(3) Is it possible to get only the bulb at the center of the cube to be on?
es.2023.1.1.rationale: Binary toggles on the cube adjacency graph.

hrt.2018.3.10.reviewed_statement:
The figure shows a chain made of $54$ unit squares. Each square, except the two end ones, is joined to its two neighbours at opposite vertices.

Each square may be placed in any position in space, provided that it stays joined to the neighbouring squares at the corresponding vertices. Is it possible to place this chain so that it forms the surface of a $3\times 3\times 3$ cube?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/croatiahmo_2018_p10_fig.png
hrt.2018.3.10.rationale: The inspected square chain must fold onto a cube surface.

no.1993.0.4.reviewed_statement: We have a cube. Each of the $8$ corners is given the value $1$ or $-1$. Each of the six faces is given a value equal to the product of its four corners. Let $A$ be the sum of the values of all the corners (eight) and all the faces (six). Then $A$ is the sum of $14$ values. Which values of $A$ are attainable?
no.1993.0.4.rationale: Products of signed vertex labels and attainable sums on a graph.

no.2009.0.1.reviewed_statement:
a. Show that there exist infinitely many integers that cannot be written as the difference between two perfect squares.

b. Show that the sum of three consecutive perfect cubes can always be written as the difference between two perfect squares.

(A perfect square is an integer raised to the second power. A perfect cube is an integer raised to the third power.)
no.2009.0.1.rationale: Integer differences of squares and sums of consecutive cube powers.

ukt.1998.1.3.reviewed_statement:
An infinite arithmetic progression, whose terms are all positive integers, contains
(i) a perfect square which is not a perfect cube, and
(ii) a perfect cube which is not a perfect square.
Prove that the arithmetic progression contains a perfect sixth power.
ukt.1998.1.3.rationale: Perfect-square/cube terms in an integer arithmetic progression.

ukt.2008.3.7.reviewed_statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be vertices of a cube. Assign the number $1$ to these vertices and $0$ to the other six vertices. A move consists of selecting a vertex, and adding $1$ to the numbers assigned to each of the three adjacent vertices. Give necessary and sufficient conditions on $M$ and $N$ for there to exist a finite sequence of moves after which all numbers assigned to the eight vertices are equal.
ukt.2008.3.7.rationale: Neighbour-addition operations and linear invariants on a cube graph.

nlt.2006.1.1.reviewed_statement:
Given a set of points in space, we may reflect a point of the set in another point of the set and add the image to the set.

If we start with a set consisting of seven of the eight vertices of a cube, can we get the eighth vertex into the set after a finite number of steps?
nlt.2006.1.1.rationale: Point reflections generate the missing cube vertex.

ch.2008.1.4.reviewed_statement: Consider three faces of an $n \times n \times n$ cube which meet at one of the vertices of the cube. For which $n$ is it possible to cover them completely and without overlap with paper strips of size $3 \times 1$? The paper strips may also be glued across the edges between these faces.
ch.2008.1.4.rationale: Strip tiling across three adjacent cube faces.

de.2013.0.2.reviewed_statement: A paper parallelogram with side lengths $25$ and $10$ and height $6$ between the longer sides is given. It is to be cut into exactly two pieces in such a way that, using both pieces, one can cover a cube of suitable edge length completely and without overlaps, without any further cuts. Describe such a cutting and show that it actually satisfies the conditions of the problem.
de.2013.0.2.rationale: Cutting and assembling a parallelogram into a cube net.

de.2017.0.4.reviewed_statement: We call a natural number heinersch if it can be written as the sum of a positive perfect square and a positive perfect cube. Prove: there are infinitely many heinersch numbers whose predecessor and successor are also heinersch.
de.2017.0.4.rationale: Neighbour relations for sums of positive square and cube powers.

dem.1968.0.2.reviewed_statement: Which of all the planes containing one and the same space diagonal of a cube with edge length $a$ cut out of the cube a cross-section of smallest area? Compute the area of such a cross-section.
dem.1968.0.2.rationale: Minimum area of a plane section through a cube diagonal.

dem.1990.0.5.reviewed_statement:
Let the vertices of a cube with given edge length $a$ be labeled $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H$ as in the figure. Let $\varepsilon_1$ be the plane in which $A, B, C, D$ lie; let $\varepsilon_2$ be the plane in which $B, C, G, F$ lie; let $g$ be the line through $H$ and the center $M$ of the square $BCGF$. Prove that among all segments which connect a point of $\varepsilon_1$ with a point of $\varepsilon_2$ and whose midpoint lies on $g$, there is a segment of smallest length. Determine this smallest length.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/demo_1990_p5_fig.png
dem.1990.0.5.rationale: The inspected diagram gives spatial planes and a minimum connecting segment.

dem.1991.0.2.reviewed_statement: For a cube-shaped box with edge length $10$ cm, consider all those lines, called marked, which pass through the interior of the cube, run parallel to an edge of the cube and have integer distances (measured in cm) from the two faces containing this edge. Prove: however the box is completely filled with $250$ rectangular building blocks of dimensions $2\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 1\text{ cm}$, there are always at least $100$ marked lines which pierce none of the blocks. Here a block counts as pierced if and only if the line contains interior points of the block.
dem.1991.0.2.rationale: Spatial block tiling and counting unpierced lines.

dem.1993.0.2.reviewed_statement: Prove that a cube can be dissected into exactly $n$ cubes for every natural number $n \ge 100$.
dem.1993.0.2.rationale: Dissecting a cube into a specified number of smaller cubes.

hkt.2008.1.2.reviewed_statement: Show that the product of three consecutive integers is the sum of four integer cubes.
hkt.2008.1.2.rationale: Representing a product of consecutive integers as a sum of third powers.

hkt.2014.1.5.rationale: Integer square conditions and differences of consecutive cube powers.

ltt.2016.2.5.reviewed_statement: An integer is written on each face of a cube. In a move it is allowed to choose any two adjacent faces and increase the numbers on them by $1$. After several moves all six numbers became equal. Determine for which initial collections of numbers this could have happened.
ltt.2016.2.5.rationale: Neighbour-increment operations on integer face labels and linear invariants.

si.2023.0.5.reviewed_statement:
On the cube $ABCDEFGH$ denote by $P$ the centre of the face $EFGH$ and by $R$ the midpoint of the edge $AB$. The plane $\Sigma$, which contains the points $C$, $P$ and $R$, intersects the edges $EF$ and $GH$ at the points $X$ and $Y$, respectively (see the figure).

a) Prove that $|EX|:|XF|=|GY|:|YH|=1:3$.

b) The plane $\Sigma$ divides the cube into two parts. Determine the ratio between the volumes of these two parts.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/slovenia_2023_p5_fig.png
si.2023.0.5.rationale: The inspected cube section determines a volume ratio.

lv.1995.0.3.reviewed_statement:
The figure CIBA consists of $4$ equal unit cubes; some of them touch along faces (see the figure).
(a) Prove that a rectangular parallelepiped can be assembled from figures CIBA.
(b) Can a cube (of any size) be assembled from figures CIBA?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/latvia_1995_p3_fig.png
lv.1995.0.3.rationale: The inspected four-cube piece tiles a box or cube.

eet.1996.0.1.reviewed_statement: The numbers $x$, $y$ and $\frac{x^2+y^2+6}{xy}$ are positive integers. Prove that $\frac{x^2+y^2+6}{xy}$ is a perfect cube.
eet.1996.0.1.rationale: Integer divisibility forces an expression to be a perfect third power.

eet.1996.0.6.reviewed_statement:
Each face of a cube is divided into $n\times n$ equal squares. The vertices of the squares are called nodes, so each face of the cube has $(n+1)^2$ nodes.
(a) For $n=2$, does there exist a closed broken line whose links are the edges of the squares which contains each node exactly once?
(b) for $n$ arbitrary, prove that each such broken line divides the surface area of the cube into two equal parts.
eet.1996.0.6.rationale: A closed lattice path on cube faces with equal-area constraints.

eet.2012.1.1.reviewed_statement: Prove that for any positive integer $k$ there exist $k$ pairwise distinct integers for which the sum of their squares equals the sum of their cubes.
eet.2012.1.1.rationale: Equality between sums of integer squares and cubes.

pt.2017.2.4.reviewed_statement: The numbers from $1$ to $8$ are placed at the vertices of a cube, one at each of the eight vertices, in such a way that the sum of the numbers at any three vertices of the same face is greater than $9$. Determine the minimum value that the sum of the numbers of one of the faces can have.
pt.2017.2.4.rationale: Vertex permutations and extremal face sums on a cube graph.

dk.2000.0.3.reviewed_statement: A GEORG MOHR cube is a cube on whose six faces the letters G, E, O, R, M and H are printed, respectively. Peter has nine identical GEORG MOHR cubes. Is it possible to stack them on top of each other into a tower which, on each of its four sides, shows the letters G E O R G M O H R in some order?
dk.2000.0.3.rationale: Letter assignment and stacking constraints on labelled cube faces.

is.2011.0.2.reviewed_statement: The vertices of a cube are numbered with the numbers from $1$ to $8$ (each number used once). For each edge, the sum of the numbers at its endpoints is formed. Is it possible to number the vertices in such a way that the sums for the edges are all different?
is.2011.0.2.rationale: Vertex permutations with distinct edge sums on a graph.

ee.2005.0.5.reviewed_statement:
A "krümbel" is the solid shown in the figure, consisting of four white unit cubes and one black unit cube. Find the smallest side length of a cube that can be filled exactly with krümbels.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/estonia_2005_p5_fig.png
ee.2005.0.5.rationale: The inspected five-cube piece must fill a larger cube.

huo.2010.0.3.reviewed_statement: We want to cover completely the three faces meeting at one vertex of a cube with edge length $k$ using $k^2$ labels of size $3 \times 1$. For which $k$ can this be done?
huo.2010.0.3.rationale: Strip tiling across three adjacent cube faces.
